title: Short Stuff: The Atlanta Washer Woman Strike
summary: Short Stuff episode on the 1881 Atlanta Washerwoman Strike. Josh opens by describing Oakland Cemetery's Halloween tour, where an actor portrayed a washerwoman involved in the strike, prompting the topic (suggested by Emily). Hosts describe post-Civil War Atlanta's push to attract northern business with cheap labor, the washerwoman trade (low pay, long hours, but relative autonomy working from home), and the 1881 formation of the Washing Society, which grew to about 3,000 members (including some white women) through door-to-door canvassing and went on strike. Police arrested six leaders; Sarah A. Collier was fined twenty dollars, refused to pay, and served forty days on a chain gang. The city then imposed a twenty-dollar annual fee and offered tax-exempt status to commercial laundries to drive the washerwomen out; the women wrote the mayor saying they would pay the fee but would stop washing clothes. Ahead of the 1881 International Cotton Exposition, other domestic workers and hotel workers joined, and the city council struck down the fees and raised wages, and reportedly gained control of the laundry industry so commercial firms could not push them out.

segments.title: Oakland Cemetery tour and how the topic was chosen
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic after learning of it on an Oakland Cemetery Halloween tour, where an actor told a washerwoman's story. Hosts briefly discuss a Stuff to Blow Your Mind colleague's cameo in a cemetery documentary and a recent show at the Eastern.
topics: Capturing the Spirit of Halloween tour

segments.title: Atlanta in the 1880s and the washerwoman trade
segments.summary: Post-Civil War Atlanta sought northern business with cheap labor. Black women, often former enslaved people, worked as laundresses for very low pay, though the work offered some independence since it was done from their own homes.

segments.title: Formation of the Washing Society and the 1881 strike
segments.summary: In summer 1881, about twenty washerwomen formed the Washing Society to demand higher pay, around a dollar per twelve pounds of wash. Door-to-door canvassing grew membership to about 3,000 in three weeks, including some white women, and they went on strike.

segments.title: Arrests, fines, and chain gang sentence
segments.summary: About ten days into the strike, police arrested six leaders on disorderly conduct and quarreling charges. Sarah A. Collier was fined twenty dollars, refused to pay, and was sentenced to forty days on a chain gang.

segments.title: City fee, letter to the mayor, and wider strikes
segments.summary: City council imposed a twenty-dollar annual fee on washerwomen and offered tax-exempt status to commercial laundries. The women wrote the mayor that they would pay but would stop washing clothes. Before the International Cotton Exposition, other domestic and hotel workers joined, and the council dropped the fees and raised wages.

segments.title: Closing thoughts and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts reflect on the women's assertion of dignity and business independence, then close the episode with the standard sign-off and an iHeartRadio production credit.
